content: Specialized guidance on sanitation in disaster situations emphasizes the importance of including sanitation as a priority in disaster preparedness planning. This involves pre-purchasing and pre-positioning sanitation and hygiene materials alongside other emergency supplies, such as those for shelter, nutrition, and health. Essential sanitation supplies include tools like picks and shovels for digging pit or trench latrines, latrine slabs or container-based sanitation cartridges, materials for constructing superstructures with privacy and lockable doors, appropriate anal cleansing materials or containers, jerry cans, handwashing stations, soap, and lime for managing fecal contamination incidents. In disaster settings, camps are often established on marginal land, which may lack adequate soil cover or have high water tables, posing significant sanitation challenges. As camps frequently evolve into urban-like settlements, long-term sanitation solutions, such as sewerage systems or fecal sludge management with effective treatment, should be considered after the immediate disaster phase. High population densities in these camps make traditional pit latrines unsustainable over extended periods. Informal or unplanned camps also require careful assessment of the impact on both displaced populations and host communities. Container-based sanitation systems can be rapidly deployed in emergencies and may also serve as long-term solutions. Sanitation planning during enteric disease outbreaks, such as cholera, requires special attention. Disinfection of feces is often impractical due to the high chlorine demand of organic material, as well as the time and cost involved. Rapid sanitation safety planning can help identify risks, prioritize actions, and monitor key interventions. Poor sanitation is a major contributing factor to enteric disease epidemics. In healthcare facilities, sanitation poses unique risks due to infectious agents and toxic chemicals. These facilities should model hygienic sanitation practices and be managed under the responsibility of the Ministry of Health. Clear job descriptions for healthcare facility managers and staff should include sanitation management responsibilities. Recommended toilet ratios are one toilet per 20 inpatients and at least two toilets for outpatients, with provisions for menstrual hygiene and accessibility for individuals with limited mobility. Toilets should be private, safe, clean, and culturally acceptable. Bedpans should only be used when necessary and handled safely with appropriate personal protective equipment to avoid spillage. Waste from bedpans and water used for cleaning them should be disposed of in toilets or the sanitation system through appropriate means, such as sluices or macerators. Handwashing facilities with soap and water should be available near toilets. All fecal waste and greywater must be fully contained. If a sewer connected to a functional treatment plant is available, these wastes can be combined and discharged into it. Otherwise, fecal waste and greywater should be conveyed separately, with fecal waste treated in an appropriately sized facility and greywater added at the secondary treatment stage. Effluent should be contained on-site through subsurface infiltration or disinfected before discharge into the environment. Effluent should never be reused, even if disinfected. A consistent budget for the operation and maintenance of healthcare facility wastewater systems is essential, and trained staff should be designated for system management and maintenance tasks. Where open defecation is prevalent, sanitation promotion and behavior change strategies should be implemented to encourage the use of existing toilets. Hygiene promotion should focus on handwashing with soap, safe disposal of child and infant feces, hygienic care of sick individuals, and treatment of drinking water supplies. Fecal sludge management should prioritize the use of licensed desludging operators, temporarily suspend tipping fees if it reduces open dumping, and enforce proper disposal practices. Operators should be required to clean serviced premises and desludging equipment with disinfectants. Behavior change is critical for improving sanitation practices. Governments play a key role in coordinating and integrating behavior change initiatives, ensuring adequate funding, and providing oversight. Sanitation behavior change strategies should be evidence-based, targeted, and include robust monitoring and feedback mechanisms. Collaboration with technical experts, universities, and social marketing agencies may be necessary to design effective programs. Understanding the determinants of sanitation behaviors is essential for designing successful interventions. These determinants may include individual knowledge, household roles and responsibilities, community norms, and contextual factors such as climate, geography, and economic conditions. Sanitation technologies also influence behavior through factors like ease of use, location, and cost. Behavior change approaches commonly used in sanitation programs include information, education, and communication (IEC) strategies, community-based approaches, social and commercial marketing, and psychological and social theories. Community-based approaches, such as Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) and Community Health Clubs (CHCs), focus on collective mobilization to create new social norms and promote improved hygiene and sanitation behaviors. These approaches are particularly effective in rural communities with high social cohesion and simpler technology needs.
